metadata.title: Continuous Batching.
metadata.note: Concept explainer (framework-first, built to pass PROOF). Topic named by request: continuous batching / processing multiple requests efficiently. Companion/zoom-in to the vLLM reel (2026-11-06), where continuous batching was one beat; here it's the whole subject. ONE reusable idea: serving many users on one GPU = keeping the batch FULL, and the enemy is WAITING — waiting to fill a batch, and waiting on the slowest request. Static (request-level) batching has both waits + head-of-line blocking; continuous (iteration-level / in-flight) batching schedules at the granularity of ONE decode step — evict finished sequences, admit waiting ones — so the batch is re-planned every token and never empties. The cost (falsifiable boundary): a joining request's PREFILL (whole prompt at once) can stall the token-by-token DECODERS for a step, and KV-cache memory caps how many sequences are live at once — so it's a throughput/tail-latency tension bounded by memory (newer schedulers add chunked prefill / prefill-decode disaggregation). Transferable test: is the server slow because the batch isn't full, or because one slow item blocks the rest? If either, schedule the smallest unit of work and let items leave/join independently. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW (verified against Orca OSDI'22 iteration-level scheduling and the continuous-batching serving literature): GPUs are throughput machines so batching amortizes a forward pass across requests (decode is memory-bandwidth bound → batching N adds little latency up to the compute-bound regime); static batching pads to and finishes at the longest sequence and blocks admission; continuous batching changes batch composition per iteration; prefill/decode interference and KV memory are the real limits. Speedups kept qualitative (several×–an order of magnitude over static) to stay durable. Bookends render via remotion at --scale=2 (4K); body B01-B04 are 4K PIL cards (make_cards.py) — kinds versus, grid, example, grid.

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. You've got one GPU and a hundred people hitting your model at once. You can't hand each of them their own GPU. So you batch, you run many requests together. But do that the obvious way, and the GPU still ends up half-idle while people wait in line. Continuous batching is the scheduling trick that fixes both. Let me show you how.

props.command: One GPU, a hundred users — how do you serve them all at once without the GPU sitting idle or everyone waiting in line?
output: batch requests to actually use the GPU
static batching stalls on the slowest

beats.narration_text: First, why batch at all. A GPU is a massively parallel machine, so running one request at a time barely uses it, and your throughput crawls. Put many requests in a batch and the GPU does all their math together, almost for the cost of doing one. So the whole game of serving is this: how full can you keep the batch? Occupancy is throughput.

card.title: One at a Time, or Batched?
card.subtitle: why serving means batching
card.caption: a GPU is a parallel machine — run requests together, or waste it
card.footer: THE GAME: KEEP THE BATCH FULL

beats.narration_text: Now the obvious way, static batching, and where it stalls. You gather a batch, then run every request in it in lockstep until the longest one finishes. But model answers vary wildly in length. So a request done in five tokens still holds its slot, padded, waiting for the one that takes five hundred. And anyone arriving mid-batch can't get in until the whole thing clears. Two kinds of waiting, and the batch moves only as fast as its slowest member.

show.at: run every request in it in lockstep

card.title: Where Static Batching Stalls.
card.subtitle: schedule the whole request at once

items.quote: short requests wait, padded, for the rest
new arrivals wait for the batch to clear

card.caption: LLM answers vary wildly in length, so the batch finishes at the pace of its slowest

beats.narration_text: Continuous batching fixes this by changing when you make the decision. Instead of scheduling a whole request at a time, you schedule one token step at a time. After every single step, the scheduler looks again: any sequence that just finished leaves immediately, freeing its slot, and a waiting request drops straight into that slot and starts generating. The batch gets re-planned every token. Nothing waits for the batch to fill, and nothing waits for the slowest to finish.

show.at: one token step at a time

card.title: Scheduled Every Step.
card.subtitle: continuous (iteration-level) batching
card.answer: finished sequences leave, freeing slots → waiting requests join immediately → the batch stays full, every step
card.caption: schedule one decode step at a time, not one whole request — no padding, no waiting to clear
card.footer: EVICT FINISHED · ADMIT WAITING · STAY FULL

beats.narration_text: It's not quite free, though. When a new request joins, the model first has to process its whole prompt in one go, that's prefill, and it's heavy. Slot that in among requests each producing a single token, and you stall the fast ones for a beat. You also need memory to hold the key-value cache for every sequence that's live at once, so memory caps how many you can batch. The real job is balancing throughput against tail latency, inside that budget.

card.title: Not Quite Free.
card.subtitle: what continuous batching costs

items.quote: a joining prompt can pause the decoders
KV cache for every live sequence
throughput vs latency, bounded by memory

card.caption: mixing a new request's prefill with everyone else's single-token decode is the hard part

beats.narration_text: So, continuous batching. Serving is keeping the GPU's batch full, and the enemy is waiting. Static batching waits to fill, and waits on the slowest. Continuous batching schedules a single token step at a time, so finished requests leave and new ones join the instant there's room. The price is juggling prefill against decode, capped by memory. But the payoff is a GPU that almost never sits idle.

props.artifactHeading: Keep the batch full, every step
artifactLines: Serving many users on one GPU means batching — running requests' math together for ~the cost of one. Throughput = batch occupancy.
Static batching waits to fill, runs lockstep to the longest request, and blocks new arrivals — the batch moves at its slowest.
Continuous batching schedules per decode step: finished sequences leave, waiting ones join immediately, so the batch stays full.
The price: a joining request's prefill can stall the decoders, and KV-cache memory caps concurrency — throughput up, tail latency to manage.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Look at any server that batches work, not just models. Ask two things. Is it slow because the batch isn't full, or because one slow item is holding everyone else up? If it's either, the fix is usually the same shape: schedule at the smallest unit of work you can, and let items leave and join the batch on their own, instead of in lockstep.
